prompts.title: Alert Triage Assistant
prompts.use_case: Triage a raw alert or log snippet and return a structured analyst verdict with MITRE mapping and next steps
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Verdict accuracy depends on alert context richness — sparse alerts produce low-confidence outputs. Always apply analyst judgment before escalating or suppressing.
prompts.prompt:
You are a SOC analyst with L2 experience performing structured alert triage.

Alert to triage:
{PASTE THE RAW ALERT, LOG LINES, OR SIEM NOTIFICATION HERE}

Analyze the alert and return ONLY the following structure. Do not add any other text.

VERDICT: [Malicious / Likely Malicious / Suspicious / Likely Benign / Benign]
CONFIDENCE: [High / Medium / Low]
REASON: [One sentence explaining the verdict]

MITRE TTPs:
- [T####.###]: [Technique Name]

SUMMARY:
[2-3 sentences describing what likely happened, what asset is at risk, and why this matters]

NEXT STEPS:
1. [Immediate action]
2. [Investigation step]
3. [Containment or follow-up]

SUPPRESSION CRITERIA: [Exact conditions under which this alert can be safely suppressed — or "Do not suppress"]

ESCALATE: [Yes / No] — [One-line reason]
prompts.example_output:
VERDICT: Likely Malicious
CONFIDENCE: Medium
REASON: PowerShell downloading a remote payload via IEX is a well-established execution pattern rarely seen in legitimate workflows.

MITRE TTPs:
- T1059.001: PowerShell
- T1105: Ingress Tool Transfer

SUMMARY:
A PowerShell process on WKSTN-042 executed an IEX(DownloadString) command pulling content from an external IP (185.220.x.x). The external IP falls in a Tor exit node range, suggesting deliberate obfuscation. The target is an end-user workstation that may now have a foothold established.

NEXT STEPS:
1. Isolate WKSTN-042 from the network immediately
2. Pull the full PowerShell command-line history and child process tree
3. Check for persistence — scheduled tasks, registry run keys, new accounts created in the past 24h

SUPPRESSION CRITERIA: Do not suppress — active download behavior to Tor infrastructure warrants investigation regardless of frequency.

ESCALATE: Yes — active potential compromise with network isolation required

variants.prompt:
You are a Tier 2 SOC analyst performing structured alert triage.

Alert:
{PASTE THE RAW ALERT HERE}

Return your analysis in this exact format only — no preamble, no commentary:

VERDICT: [Malicious / Likely Malicious / Suspicious / Likely Benign / Benign]
CONFIDENCE: [High / Medium / Low]
REASON: [One sentence]
MITRE TTPs: [comma-separated T#### IDs and names]
SUMMARY: [2-3 sentences]
NEXT STEPS: [numbered list, max 3]
SUPPRESSION CRITERIA: [one line or "Do not suppress"]
ESCALATE: [Yes/No — one-line reason]
variants.notes: GPT-4o adds a preamble before VERDICT — "no preamble, no commentary" reduces it. Still sometimes reformats the MITRE field, watch for it.

prompts.title: Sigma Rule Generator
prompts.use_case: Generate a valid Sigma rule from a plain-English description of an attack behavior
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: Hallusinates field names for uncommon log sources — always validate detection fields against your SIEM schema before deployment
prompts.prompt:
You are a detection engineer with deep expertise in Sigma rule authoring.

Attack behavior to detect:
{DESCRIBE THE ATTACK BEHAVIOR IN PLAIN ENGLISH}

Write a valid Sigma rule that detects this behavior. Follow these requirements exactly:
- Use standard Sigma YAML structure: title, id, status, description, references, author, date, tags, logsource, detection, falsepositives, level
- Set status to "experimental"
- Choose the most specific logsource available (product, service, or category)
- Write detection logic using keywords, selection, and condition fields
- Use field names from common log sources (Windows Event Log, Sysmon, auditd, etc.)
- Include at least two realistic false positive scenarios
- Set an appropriate level: informational | low | medium | high | critical
- Add MITRE ATT&CK tags in format: attack.tXXXX and attack.tactic

Output ONLY the Sigma rule in YAML. No explanation, no markdown fences, no commentary.
prompts.example_output:
title: Suspicious PowerShell Encoded Command Execution
id: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of PowerShell with base64-encoded commands, commonly used by attackers to obfuscate malicious payloads
references:
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
author: hrushikesh-badgujar
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1027
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-EncodedCommand'
      - '-enc '
      - '-ec '
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate administrative scripts using encoded commands
  - Software installers that invoke encoded PowerShell during setup
level: medium

variants.prompt:
You are a detection engineer. Generate a Sigma rule to detect the following attack behavior:

{DESCRIBE THE ATTACK BEHAVIOR IN PLAIN ENGLISH}

Rules:
1. Use valid Sigma YAML format with all required fields
2. status: experimental
3. Include realistic MITRE ATT&CK tags (attack.tXXXX)
4. Use specific logsource — do not use "generic"
5. Write a condition that minimizes false positives
6. List two false positive scenarios
7. Output ONLY the YAML. No explanation.
variants.notes: GPT-4o adds markdown code fences and preamble by default — the explicit "Output ONLY the YAML" helps but still verify field names against your schema.

variants.prompt:
Task: Write a Sigma detection rule for the attack behavior below.

Attack behavior:
{DESCRIBE THE ATTACK BEHAVIOR IN PLAIN ENGLISH}

Output format — return ONLY this YAML structure, nothing else:

title: [rule title]
id: [generate a UUID]
status: experimental
description: [one sentence]
tags:
  - attack.[tactic]
  - attack.t[technique_id]
logsource:
  category: [process_creation|network_connection|file_event|etc]
  product: [windows|linux|macos]
detection:
  selection:
    [field]: [value]
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - [scenario 1]
  - [scenario 2]
level: [informational|low|medium|high|critical]
variants.notes: Llama adds prose between YAML fields without an explicit skeleton. Providing the structure directly produces clean output.

prompts.title: Threat Intel Summarizer
prompts.use_case: Extract structured, SOC-ready intelligence from a raw threat report, blog post, or advisory
prompts.author: hrushikesh-badgujar
prompts.limitations: May miss obfuscated indicators (defanged URLs, hex-encoded IPs) — scan the output manually. Does not replace dedicated IOC extraction tools like PARSE-X.
prompts.prompt:
You are a threat intelligence analyst preparing a structured intelligence summary for SOC distribution.

Threat report:
{PASTE THE FULL THREAT REPORT, BLOG POST, OR ADVISORY HERE}

Extract and return ONLY the following. Write "Not mentioned" for any field with no data.

THREAT ACTOR: [Name or "Unknown"]
MOTIVATION: [Financial / Espionage / Hacktivism / Destructive / Unknown]
TARGETS: [Industries, geographies, or named organizations]
ACTIVE SINCE: [Date or "Unknown"]

TTPs:
- [T####.###] [Technique Name]: [How the actor used it — one sentence]

INDICATORS OF COMPROMISE:
- IPs: [one per line]
- Domains: [one per line]
- File Hashes: [hash type + value, one per line]
- URLs: [one per line]
- Email Addresses: [one per line]

DETECTION OPPORTUNITIES:
- [Specific log source or behavior to hunt for — max 5]

HUNTING HYPOTHESES:
- [Specific, testable hypothesis — max 3]

RECOMMENDED MITIGATIONS:
- [CVE ID or security control — one per line]

PRIORITY: [Critical / High / Medium / Low] — [One-line rationale]
prompts.example_output:
THREAT ACTOR: Lazarus Group (aka HIDDEN COBRA)
MOTIVATION: Financial
TARGETS: Cryptocurrency exchanges, DeFi platforms — primarily Southeast Asia and Europe
ACTIVE SINCE: 2009

TTPs:
- T1566.002 Spearphishing Link: Sent lure emails with job offer PDFs linking to weaponized Google Drive documents
- T1059.001 PowerShell: Executed encoded commands post-phishing to pull second-stage payload
- T1055.012 Process Hollowing: Injected payload into legitimate svchost.exe to evade EDR detection

INDICATORS OF COMPROMISE:
- IPs:
  185.220.101.45
  91.108.4.77
- Domains:
  update-service[.]net
  cdn-delivery[.]org
- File Hashes:
  SHA256: a3f1b2c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d7e8f9a0b1c2d3e4f5a6b7c8d9e0f1a2
- URLs:
  hxxps://update-service[.]net/payload.bin
- Email Addresses: Not mentioned

DETECTION OPPORTUNITIES:
- PowerShell spawned by Outlook or browser processes (parent-child chain)
- Outbound connections to domains registered within the past 30 days from workstations
- svchost.exe executing from non-System32 paths

HUNTING HYPOTHESES:
- Finance-team workstations made outbound connections to newly registered domains in the past 30 days
- PowerShell with encoded commands executed within 1 hour of an email open event
- svchost.exe instances with unusual parent processes (not services.exe)

RECOMMENDED MITIGATIONS:
- Disable Office macros from internet-sourced documents via GPO
- Block outbound connections to domains registered less than 30 days ago at the proxy
- Deploy AppLocker to restrict PowerShell from user-writable paths

PRIORITY: High — active financial sector targeting with well-documented TTPs and high detection confidence
